script.scamName: Fake FTC agent phone cutoff call

message.body: FTC: Agent Badge ID 4471-B. A phone registered under your name is being used for scams overseas. Your number will be deactivated unless you cooperate. Do not discuss this case with anyone. A police officer will contact you to file a report.
message.provenanceNote: The FTC Consumer Alert describes this scheme as a phone call from someone claiming to be an FTC official. The call's claims (the badge ID, the phone-registered-in-your-name story, the deactivation threat, the secrecy demand, and the handoff to a fake police officer) are adapted into a text message here so they can be shown on the screen.

evidence.quote: someone claiming to be an FTC official (who’s really a scammer) calls to say a phone was registered under your name and number and is being used to commit scams in another country.
If you don’t cooperate, they threaten to deactivate your phone number.
the FTC impersonator will transfer you to a (fake) police officer to file a report.

script.hook: Real or scam? You get three seconds.
script.stampSay: Scam. The FTC won't cut you off.

flags.label: Phone cutoff threat
flags.say: They scare you by saying your number will be shut off.

evidence.quote: A real FTC employee will never ever threaten to disconnect your phone. That’s a scam.

flags.label: Keep it secret
flags.say: A real FTC employee never tells you to keep your conversations secret.

target.match: Do not discuss this case with anyone

evidence.quote: A real FTC employee will never ever tell you to keep your conversations secret. That’s always a scam.

flags.label: Fake badge number
flags.say: That badge ID is fake and meant to sound official.

evidence.quote: The “FTC official” even reads off their badge ID (it’s a fake badge).

safeMove.label: Report it
safeMove.say: Tell the FTC about it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

evidence.quote: Spot one of these scams? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the FTC Consumer Alerts post, which describes paid ads with lookalike government web addresses, official-looking logos, and a link or phone number inside the ad.

evidence.quote: But before you click on a search result, remember: scammers and dishonest businesses sometimes pay to appear at the top.

If you use the link or phone number in the ad, you might end up paying for a scammy plan that’s not health insurance, or expose yourself to medical identity theft.

message.body: Transcript: Hi, this is Dana from the Example Charity Fund. Because you donated last year, you were entered in our donor sweepstakes, and you won the $25,000 grand prize! To release the funds, we just need a $299 processing fee and your Social Security number to verify you. Call us back today at (202) 555-0147. Congratulations!
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from the FTC Consumer Alerts article, which describes calls from someone claiming to be with a charity you support, saying you won a sweepstakes and asking you to pay or give your Social Security number. The charity name is clearly fictional and does not refer to any real organization.

evidence.quote: these impersonators sometimes make you believe that you won a charity-sponsored sweepstakes because you’ve donated to that charity.
Only scammers demand you pay or give them personal information like your Social Security number to get a prize.

script.hook: A voicemail says you won. Read it.
script.stampSay: Won a prize? Then why pay?

flags.label: Pay to claim
flags.say: They want money before you get the prize, and that alone means scam.

evidence.quote: The moment someone tells you to pay to claim your prize, you know you’re dealing with a scam.

flags.label: Asks for your Social
flags.say: Only a scammer asks for your Social Security number to hand over a prize.

target.match: Social Security number to verify you

evidence.quote: Only scammers demand you pay or give them personal information like your Social Security number to get a prize.

flags.label: Faked caller ID
flags.say: The name and number on your screen can be faked, so do not trust them.

evidence.quote: Scammers can fake caller ID. Don’t trust it, even if it shows a real government agency or company name or phone number.

safeMove.label: Search, skip the ads
safeMove.say: Search the charity name with the word scam, and scroll past the paid ads first.

evidence.quote: Search online for the name of the contest or company with words like “complaint,” “review,” or “scam” to see what others are saying. But don’t rely on the first search results you see. Sometimes imposters advertise on platforms like Google Search and Bing to lead you to false information. Scroll past the paid ads to help avoid these imposters.

message.subject: Please verify your login
message.body:
Your login for the county election portal needs a check. Please verify your login now: https://portal-verify.example/login

Thank you,
Portal Team
message.provenanceNote: Recreated from Source 1 (FBI IC3 PSA), which describes phishing emails that closely resemble legitimate communications, push targets to click malicious links, and try to get them to disclose login credentials. The exact wording, sender name and portal name are invented for this example.

evidence.quote: Malicious cyber actors may attempt to disrupt the 2026 U.S. midterm elections using phishing and smishing techniques to steal user data, including login credentials and sensitive information.

In recent years, these actors have crafted increasingly sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications, making it difficult for targets to distinguish fraudulent messages.

script.hook: This email wants your password. Would you tap this?
script.stampSay: This one is after your login.

flags.label: Looks like real mail
flags.say: These fakes are built to look like real messages, so they are hard to spot.

evidence.quote: In recent years, these actors have crafted increasingly sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications, making it difficult for targets to distinguish fraudulent messages.

flags.label: Asks for login
flags.say: The whole point is to trick you into giving up your login details.

evidence.quote: Such precautions are critical to remaining vigilant for phishing and smishing attempts that try to manipulate the recipient into disclosing sensitive information, such as login credentials or financial information, or that install malware on their devices.

flags.label: Link to tap
flags.say: That link is the trap, and real-sounding words make clicking it more likely.

evidence.quote: SI allows malicious cyber actors to create language that appears genuine, using native languages and common vernacular, making it more likely for potential victims to click malicious links or inadvertently expose information through direct interaction with threat actors.

safeMove.label: Confirm another way
safeMove.say: Before you share any login, confirm the request through a separate channel you trust.

evidence.quote: Employees should confirm, if possible, requests for sensitive information through secondary channels.

skipped.reason: problems: The 'Badge photo proof' flag targets an attachment, but the message has none. The body only states a badge ID number in text. The flag points at nothing on screen.

problems: Flag 1 'say' ('No real investment hands you a set profit every single week') is a general claim about all legitimate investments. The quote only says NovaTech advertised about 2-4% per week. The source never says fixed weekly returns are impossible for real investments.

problems: Flag 'Friendly mentor': the say line 'then drain everything' is not supported by the attached quote, which only covers mentors building trust. The source does say scammers 'ultimately vanish with all the victim's money,' but that line is not the cited evidence. Either swap the quote or soften the say line.

problems: provenanceNote says the source describes a follow-up text with a fake employee ID photo 'that the source says scammers send.' The source never says scammers in this scheme text a photo. It only says a real FTC employee will never text a photo of their employee ID. In the source, the badge ID is read aloud on the call. The note should not attribute this to the source.

problems: The 'Faith used as bait' flag targets the sender with an empty match string, so it highlights nothing specific. The religious appeal is in the body ('God has opened a door for us'), so the flag should target that text.
problems: Flag 'Friendly stranger mentor' has target kind 'sender' with an empty match string, so it does not point at the sender 'Coach Daniel'.
problems: safeMove label 'Keep your crypto' is advice the source never gives. The source only reports that investors could not withdraw when NovaTech collapsed; it offers no protective guidance.

problems: The hook "Would you tap this pop-up while browsing?" and the phone-screen framing suggest a mobile tap threat. The source describes keyboard commands (Windows + R, Ctrl + V, Enter), which only work on a Windows computer, and tapping is not the risky action. Viewers could misjudge where and how this attack works.
